post.summary: Authenticates a user and issues an access token plus a refresh token.
post.description:
Open to anonymous callers and rate limited to 10 requests per minute (fixed window,
shared by all callers of the auth endpoints). Token lifetimes come from configuration:
`Jwt:AccessTokenExpirationMinutes` (15) and `Jwt:RefreshTokenExpirationDays` (7).
Only a SHA-256 hash of the refresh token is persisted, so the raw value is returned here once.

200.description: Access token, refresh token, the access token's UTC expiry and the username.

post.summary: Exchanges a refresh token for a new access token and a new refresh token.
post.description:
Open to anonymous callers (the refresh token itself is the credential) and rate limited
like login. Refresh tokens rotate: the presented token is revoked and its replacement
stored in the same save, so a token can only be redeemed once. Presenting an already
rotated token is treated as theft and revokes every refresh token of that user.

200.description: A new access token, a new refresh token and the access token's UTC expiry.

post.summary: Revokes the supplied refresh token, ending that one session.
post.description:
Other sessions of the same user keep working. Access tokens are validated by signature
and lifetime only, so an already issued access token stays usable until it expires.

post.summary: Revokes every refresh token of the calling user, ending all their sessions.
post.description:
The user is taken from the access token's subject claim. As with a single logout,
access tokens already handed out remain valid until they expire.

get.summary: Reports whether this instance still has no user account and needs the initial setup.

200.description: `needsSetup` — true while not a single user exists.

post.summary: Creates the first user account and signs it in.
post.description:
Open to anonymous callers, but only while the instance has no user at all — once one
exists the call is rejected. The password must be at least 8 characters long.

200.description: The same token set as a login: access token, refresh token, expiry and username.

get.summary: All saved selections, ordered by name.

put.summary: Saves a selection under a name; an existing one with that name is overwritten.
put.description:
The name is trimmed and matched case-insensitively, so saving "pumpe" updates "Pumpe" (and
adopts the new spelling). Addresses are trimmed and de-duplicated, keeping their order.
Validation: the name must be 1 to 100 characters, and there must be 1 to 8 addresses of at most
20 characters each, otherwise 400 and nothing is stored.

get.summary: Recent log entries from the in-memory buffer, optionally filtered.
Availability of the recording: when did the monitor run, and was the bus link up.
get.description:
Answers the question a hole in the telegram history cannot: a stretch reported as
`Up` was genuinely quiet on the bus, `BusDown` means the link was gone, and
`MonitorDown` means the process was not running (restart, standby, crash). Derived from
the one-per-minute heartbeats, so boundaries are accurate to about one minute. Stretches the
record does not cover — before the first beat was ever written, or past its retention —
report as `Unknown` and are deliberately not counted as outages.
The range is clamped to now, because the future is neither up nor down.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Start (UTC). Defaults to seven days before to.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: End (UTC). Defaults to now; a later value is clamped to now.

get.summary: Downloads a diagnostics zip: recent log files + a system-info.json.
App version (for support / bug reports).
Current state of the KNX bus link.
get.description:
Read-only — nothing is sent to the bus. Configuration is the configuration the live link
was established with and is null while disconnected; it is not necessarily the stored
configuration flagged active. ManualDisconnect is latched by a manual disconnect and keeps
the auto-connect worker from reconnecting until the next connect clears it.

200.description:
Connection flag, link state (Disconnected / Connecting / Connected), the
    manual-disconnect latch, the configuration currently in use, and recording health
    (link timestamps plus drop counters, both reset on restart).

post.summary: Opens the KNX bus link using the stored configuration with the given id.
post.description:
Touches the installation: an IP tunnel is opened (or the routing multicast group joined),
and received telegrams start flowing into the live view and the history again. An existing
link is torn down first. Clears the manual-disconnect latch, so the auto-connect worker may
keep the link up from here on. The request body is the bare configuration id (a JSON number).
Unknown id yields 404, a failed connect 400.

Ends telegram recording until the next connect. Latches manual-disconnect so the
auto-connect worker does not reconnect on its own; the next connect (or enabling
auto-connect) clears the latch. Succeeds even when no link is currently up.

post.summary:
Probes whether a stored configuration can reach the bus. Sends no group telegram and
changes nothing in the stored configuration.
post.description:
The probe uses a throwaway connection. If a live link is currently up it is paused for the
duration of the probe (freeing the gateway's tunnel slot) and restored afterwards, so
recording has a short gap — the frontend warns before triggering this while live.
For routing configurations the probe additionally listens up to five seconds for real bus
traffic: joining a multicast group succeeds locally even when no telegram can ever arrive.
That case is reported as JoinedWithoutTraffic and counts as a warning, not a failure
(Success stays true). Unknown id yields 404.

200.description: Success flag (false only for Failed), the outcome and a human-readable message.

get.summary:
Auto-connect state for the effective configuration (active one, else the first).
The active project is coupled to the bus link, so this governs whether it auto-connects.
get.description:
Read-only. When no configuration is stored at all, Enabled is reported as true (the default
for a configuration that has yet to be created).

200.description: The auto-connect flag and whether a bus link is currently up.

put.summary: Enables or disables auto-connect for the effective configuration.
put.description:
Applied immediately, not merely stored: enabling opens the bus link right away when none is
up (which clears the manual-disconnect latch), disabling closes an existing link. A failed
immediate connect is not reported as an error — the auto-connect worker retries on its next
tick (roughly every ten seconds). 404 when no configuration is stored.

200.description: The stored flag and whether a bus link is up afterwards.

post.summary:
Sends a GroupValueWrite to the bus. ⚠ Writes to the real KNX installation — the frontend
gates this behind an explicit confirmation dialog.
post.description:
This has a physical effect: the addressed actuators act on the value. The value is encoded
with the given datapoint type; without a DatapointType only a raw hex string ("0x01",
"01 02") is accepted, anything else is rejected. Answers 400 with Success=false when the
address is missing or unparsable, when no bus link is up, or when the value could not be
encoded for the given DPT.

post.summary: Sends a GroupValueRead; the response shows up as a normal telegram.
post.description:
Puts a telegram on the real installation, but changes no value — the addressed device
answers with its current one. The answering GroupValueResponse arrives through the normal
receive path and appears in the live view and the history; this endpoint itself only
confirms that the request was sent, it does not return the value. Answers 400 with
Success=false when the address is missing or unparsable, or when no bus link is up.

post.summary: Stores a new KNX interface configuration.
post.description:
Storing alone does not touch the bus: the entry is created inactive and no connection is
opened here. Connect explicitly, or leave AutoConnect on — the auto-connect worker picks a
configuration only while no link is up, preferring the active one, else the first with
AutoConnect enabled. Tunneling accepts a host name as well as an IP address; routing needs a
multicast IP. The tunnel options (protocol, requested address, IP Secure) are ignored for routing.

200.description: The stored configuration including its assigned id.

get.summary: Lists all stored KNX interface configurations.
Returns a single stored KNX interface configuration.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Id of the stored configuration; 404 when it does not exist.

put.summary: Updates a stored KNX interface configuration; may re-establish the live bus link.
put.description:
When the connection actually changes (address, port, connection type or one of the tunnel
options), the configuration has AutoConnect enabled and a link is currently up, the running
connection is re-opened with the new settings — that briefly interrupts recording. Changing
only the physical address or the auto-connect flag does not trigger a reconnect. A failed
reconnect is not an error: the response reports Reconnected=false and the auto-connect
worker retries.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Id of the stored configuration; 404 when it does not exist.

requestBody.description: The new values — same payload shape as when creating a configuration.

200.description: The stored configuration and whether the live link was re-established.

post.summary: Uploads an ETS project file and starts the import as a background job.
post.description:
Returns as soon as the job exists — the parse itself runs in the background, so poll
`GET imports/{id}` for progress. Only files ending in `.knxproj` are accepted,
and the request body is capped at 200 MB.

If the archive is password protected the job stops in `WaitingForInput` and lists what
it needs; feed those inputs to `POST imports/{id}/provide-input`, then the job continues
on its own. Re-uploading a project that was imported before is recognised by its ETS project
id and updates the existing project in place, so recorded telegrams keep their group-address
link. A genuinely new project is auto-activated when no other project is active yet.

200.description: The created import job: id, status, the step list and (once finished) the project id and counts.

get.summary: Returns the current state of an import job.
get.description:
Jobs are held in memory only. A job that has completed, failed or been cancelled is swept
an hour after it terminated (the cleanup worker runs every five minutes) and is reported as
not found from then on.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Job id returned by the upload call.

200.description: Status, overall progress, per-step detail and the outstanding requirements.

delete.summary: Marks an import job as cancelled.
delete.description:
This flips the job state only. A parse already running in the background is not interrupted
and a project it has written stays. Unknown job ids are accepted without effect.

post.summary: Supplies one requested input — project password, keyring file or keyring password — to a waiting import job.
post.description:
Each call fulfils exactly the requirement named in `type`; the keyring file is passed
Base64-encoded. The call is only accepted while the job is in `WaitingForInput` and
rejected otherwise.

Supplying the project password triggers a second look inside the now decryptable archive:
if KNX Secure devices turn up, an optional keyring file and keyring password requirement are
added and the job stays in `WaitingForInput`. As soon as every listed requirement is
marked fulfilled, the import resumes in the background — poll `GET imports/{id}` from
there. The password is not verified at this point; a wrong one surfaces as a failed job.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Job id of the waiting import.

requestBody.description: The values for the requirements the job is waiting on.

get.summary: Lists all imported projects.

200.description: Per project: name, source file name, import date, active flag and the group-address and device counts.

get.summary: Returns one project together with its group addresses and devices.
get.description: Both lists come back complete and unpaged, so the response grows with the size of the project.

delete.summary: Deletes a project and everything parsed from it.
delete.description:
Removes the project's group addresses, devices, locations, communication objects, group
ranges and stored keyring material in one transaction. Recorded telegrams are kept but lose
their group-address link and are shown undecoded from then on. Deleting the active project
leaves no project active; the bus link stays up.

put.summary: Makes this project the active one.
put.description:
Activation is exclusive: any other active project is deactivated in the same transaction,
so at most one project is ever active. Afterwards the group-address cache is refreshed and
incoming telegrams resolve to this project's names and DPTs. The bus connection is
deliberately left untouched — activating decodes, it does not connect.

put.summary: Deactivates the project, leaving no project active.
put.description:
The group-address cache is cleared, so telegrams are shown undecoded — raw hex, without name
or DPT. Monitoring keeps running: the bus link stays up. Deactivating a project that is
already inactive succeeds and changes nothing.

get.summary: Reports what deleting this project would affect, for the confirmation dialog.

200.description:
The project's group-address and device counts plus the number of recorded telegrams mapped
to it. Those telegrams survive the deletion — they only lose their group-address mapping.

get.summary: Returns the project's locations (buildings, floors, rooms, …).
get.description:
A flat list, not a tree — the hierarchy is expressed through each entry's parent id. Every
entry also carries the device and group addresses assigned to that location.

get.summary: Returns the project's communication objects, optionally only those linked to one group address.
get.description:
Each entry is enriched with the name, manufacturer and product name of the device behind its
physical address, as far as that device is part of the project. Sorted by device address,
then by object number.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Project id.

parameters.name: address
parameters.description: Group address (`m/m/s`). When set, only objects whose group-address link matches it exactly are returned.

get.summary: Returns the project's group ranges — the named main and middle groups — ordered by range start.
Resolves a single device of the project by its physical address.
get.description:
The address is matched exactly, and an unknown project id is reported the same way as an
unknown device.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Project id.

parameters.name: address
parameters.description: Physical address (`a.l.d`) to look up. Required.

post.summary: Attaches a keyring (`.knxkeys`) to an already imported project.
post.description:
Multipart upload of the file plus its password; both are required and only files ending in
`.knxkeys` are accepted. Any keyring material previously stored for the project is
replaced — both the decrypted per-key rows and the raw keyring bytes, which KNX Data Secure
needs when it loads the keyring at connect time. Because of that the keyring password is
stored with the project. A wrong password or an unreadable file is reported as a client error.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Project the keyring belongs to.

requestBody.description: Password of the keyring file. Required.

200.description: How many keys were read, split into group-address and tool keys, and whether a backbone key is present.

get.summary: Current recording settings: hot-buffer size and cold-archive options.
get.description:
Served from the cached snapshot that the recording services themselves read, so this needs
no database round-trip.

put.summary: Updates the recording settings; they take effect on the running recording.
put.description:
The values are persisted and swapped into the snapshot the recording workers read, so no
restart is needed. What the fields do:
HotBufferMaxCount is the number of telegrams kept in the database — a retention pass
periodically deletes everything older than the newest HotBufferMaxCount rows, so lowering
the value discards the oldest telegrams. Deletion happens chunked on the following passes,
not the instant the value is saved.
ArchiveEnabled toggles the additional NDJSON+gzip day-files; switching it off stops new
writes but leaves existing archive files untouched.
ArchiveRetentionDays deletes archive day-files older than that many days, null keeps them
forever. The sweep runs at startup and at the daily file rollover, so a shortened retention
only takes effect at the next sweep.
HistoryWriteIntervalSeconds collects telegrams for that long and writes them to the history
in one transaction (0 = right away). It spares SD cards and eMMC; a power cut loses what is
still buffered, the live view is not delayed. The NDJSON archive syncs on the same rhythm.
Validation: HotBufferMaxCount must be greater than 0, ArchiveRetentionDays must be null or
greater than 0, HistoryWriteIntervalSeconds 0 to 600 — otherwise 400 and nothing is changed.

200.description: The settings as they are now in effect.

get.summary:
Numeric time-series per destination group address. Each telegram's decoded value is
projected to a number (leading numeric token, else On/Off-style boolean → 1/0); telegrams
that yield no number are skipped. The result is down-sampled to at most maxPoints per address.
get.description:
A number is taken from the decoded value as the first numeric token (leading minus and
    decimal point or comma allowed), so "21.5 °C" becomes 21.5; failing that, a known
    boolean-ish word (On/Off, True/False, Open/Closed, Up/Down, …) becomes 1 or 0. Anything
    else is dropped, and an address whose telegrams yield no number at all is omitted from the
    response instead of appearing empty. `unit` is whatever remains of the first chartable
    sample once the number is stripped — "°C" for "21.5 °C"; for a boolean sample, which holds
    no number to strip, the word itself remains.
    Down-sampling keeps the minimum and the maximum of each bucket rather than every n-th
point, so spikes survive a wide range. maxPoints is the budget per address, not the
exact count — the result may be shorter, and downSampled plus totalPoints
(the numeric points before down-sampling) report what happened.
    At most 200 000 rows are read per request. When the range holds more, the newest
rows win, the older end is missing and truncated is true — a chart is easier to
distrust when it starts late than when it ends early.
    carry is the last chartable value before from (with its original
timestamp), so a client can draw the curve from the left edge instead of starting it at
the first telegram inside the range, since a KNX value holds until the next telegram. It is null
when there is no earlier value, and always null when truncated is true, since the
missing older end would sit between it and the first point. An address with a carry value
but no telegram inside the range is returned with an empty points list.
    A timestamp without a zone designator (from=2026-07-30T00:00:00) is interpreted as
server local time, not UTC. Send ISO-8601 with a trailing Z to be unambiguous.
Returned point timestamps are always UTC with a trailing Z.

parameters.name: addresses
parameters.description:
Comma-separated destination group addresses (e.g. `1/2/3,1/2/4`). Duplicates are
dropped and at most the first 8 are used; the rest are silently ignored. Missing or empty
yields an empty series list rather than an error.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Start of the range (inclusive). Defaults to 24 hours before `to`.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: End of the range (inclusive). Defaults to now. A reversed range is swapped, not rejected.

parameters.name: maxPoints
parameters.description: Maximum points returned per address after down-sampling. Default 2000, clamped to 1..10000.

200.description:
One entry per requested address that has chartable data, in the order the addresses were
requested, plus a `truncated` flag for the whole request.

get.summary:
Telegram volume histogram over [from,to] split into buckets equal buckets,
plus the total count. Backs the statistics "telegrams over time" / msg-per-second view.
get.description:
Counts all telegrams in the range — there is no address, source or type filter here. Every
    bucket is returned, including empty ones, so the buckets always tile the range gap-free.
    `bucketMs` is the bucket width in milliseconds and is fractional: the range is divided
    into equal parts rather than snapped to a round interval, and each bucket's `t` is its
    start. Divide a count by `bucketMs` to get a rate.
    A timestamp without a zone designator is interpreted as server local time, not UTC. Send
ISO-8601 with a trailing Z to be unambiguous.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Start of the range (inclusive). Defaults to 24 hours before `to`.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: End of the range (inclusive). Defaults to now. A reversed range is swapped, not rejected.

parameters.name: buckets
parameters.description: Number of equal-width buckets. Default 60, clamped to 1..500.

get.summary:
Activity heatmap: telegram counts bucketed by (weekday, hour-of-day) over [from,to].
Binning is done in the caller's local time via tz (minutes the local
zone is behind UTC, i.e. JS getTimezoneOffset()), so "18:00 Monday" means the user's 18:00.
get.description:
The grid is always 7 × 24 (weekday 0 = Sunday .. 6 = Saturday, then hour 0..23) and is
    filled with counts, not averages: a 30-day range puts roughly four Mondays into the same
    cell. Counts all telegrams in the range — there is no address, source or type filter.
    A timestamp without a zone designator is interpreted as server local time, not UTC. Send
ISO-8601 with a trailing Z to be unambiguous. Note that tz shifts only the
binning, not the range boundaries.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Start of the range (inclusive). Defaults to 24 hours before `to`.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: End of the range (inclusive). Defaults to now. A reversed range is swapped, not rejected.

parameters.name: tz
parameters.description:
Minutes the display zone is behind UTC, exactly as JavaScript's
`Date.getTimezoneOffset()` reports it (CEST = -120). Default 0 bins in UTC. A fixed
offset is applied to the whole range, so a range spanning a DST change is binned with one
offset throughout.

get.summary:
The busiest destination group addresses and the busiest senders over [from,to], for the
bus-load breakdown in the statistics view.
get.description:
Both lists are ranked by telegram count, highest first, ties broken by address, and hold
    at most limit entries each. `share` is the percentage of all
    telegrams in the range (`total`), `perHour` the count divided by the length of
    the range in hours (`rangeHours`), so a short range is not mistaken for a quiet one.
    Names and DPTs come from the currently active project: an address that is not part
of it, or a range recorded under an older project, shows whatever today's project says,
or null. Counts all telegrams in the range, every message type included.
    A timestamp without a zone designator is interpreted as server local time, not UTC. Send
ISO-8601 with a trailing Z to be unambiguous.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Start of the range (inclusive). Defaults to 24 hours before `to`.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: End of the range (inclusive). Defaults to now. A reversed range is swapped, not rejected.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Entries per list. Default 20, clamped to 1..100.

get.summary: Keyset-paginated telegram history (newest first).
get.description:
Reads the database hot tier only — the day archive on disk is served by the
    `archive/*` endpoints. Filters: `from`/`to`, `address` (destination
    group address), `source` (individual address), `type` or `types`
    (comma-separated, OR-combined and taking precedence over `type`) and `q`
    (free-text LIKE across source, destination, decoded value, GA name and DPT).
    Paging is keyset-based over (Timestamp, Id), not offset-based: pass the nextCursor
of the previous response as cursor to get the following page. The cursor is opaque;
a malformed one yields 400. pageSize defaults to 100 and is clamped to 1..1000.
order=asc sorts oldest first, any other value newest first — the sort direction must
stay the same while paging, because the cursor is interpreted relative to it.
    from/to are compared against the stored UTC timestamps without any conversion
(unlike the chart endpoints), so pass UTC values.

200.description:
One page of telegrams plus `hasMore` and `nextCursor`; `nextCursor` is null
on the last page.

delete.summary: Permanently deletes the entire telegram history (the DB hot-tier). Irreversible.
delete.description:
Deletes every row in one statement — the request carries no filter, so there is no way to
clear only part of the history. The SQLite WAL is checkpointed afterwards so the file
shrinks. Archive files on disk are not touched and stay downloadable.

200.description: An object with a single `deleted` property: the number of rows removed.

get.summary: Number of telegrams matching a filter.
get.description:
Takes the same query parameters as `GET /api/telegrams`, but only the filtering ones
have an effect — `cursor`, `pageSize` and `order` are ignored. Counts the
database hot tier only.

200.description: An object with a single `count` property.

get.summary: Server-streamed CSV export over the full filtered DB range.
get.description:
Accepts the same filters as `GET /api/telegrams`, but exports every matching row:
    `cursor` and `pageSize` are ignored and there is no row limit. Rows are always
    written chronologically (oldest first), regardless of `order`.
    The response is streamed while the query is still running, so the body starts arriving
before the row count is known and no Content-Length is sent. The header line is
always written, even when nothing matches. Encoding is UTF-8 without BOM; fields that
contain a comma, quote or line break are quoted with doubled inner quotes. The filename is
knx-telegrams-{UTC timestamp}.csv.
    Columns: Timestamp, SourceAddress, SourceName, SourceLocation, DestinationAddress, GroupAddressName,
Functions, DatapointType, MessageType, Value, ValueDecoded. SourceLocation is the sender's full
building path ("Building › Floor › Room"), Functions the ETS functions of the destination
joined by "; "; both resolve against the active project like SourceName. Value is the raw payload as uppercase hex without
separators. Timestamp is the UTC value in ISO-8601 round-trip format but carries no
zone designator — unlike the JSON responses, which end in Z. GroupAddressName and
DatapointType are empty when the telegram has no linked group address; SourceName is empty
when the sender is not a device of the active project.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: Only `csv` is supported; any other value yields 400.

get.summary: Lists the days available in the cold-tier archive, newest first.
get.description:
The archive holds one NDJSON file per UTC day, written independently of the database hot
tier and unaffected by its retention or by `DELETE /api/telegrams`. Finished days are
gzipped (`compressed: true`), the current day stays plain and is still being appended
to, so its size grows between calls. `sizeBytes` is the size on disk, i.e. the
compressed size for gzipped days. Archiving is opt-in via the recording settings, so the
list is empty as long as nothing has been archived.

200.description: One entry per day with `date` (YYYY-MM-DD), `fileName`, `sizeBytes` and `compressed`.

get.summary: Downloads the raw archive file of one UTC day.
get.description:
Serves the gzipped file (`application/gzip`) when it exists and falls back to the
plain, still-open file of the current day (`application/x-ndjson`); 404 when neither
is present for that day. The payload is NDJSON — one JSON object per line with the keys
`t` (UTC timestamp), `s` (source address), `d` (destination address),
`mt` (message type), `r` (raw value) and `v` (decoded value, omitted when
there is none). The current day is served while the writer still holds it open, so it can
be missing the last few seconds — the writer flushes on an interval.

parameters.name: date
parameters.description: Archive day as `YYYY-MM-DD` (UTC). Any other shape yields 400.
